title: Point-UQ: Uncertainty-Guided 3D Learning Without Retraining
one_liner: When learning new 3D object classes from a few examples, use uncertainty—a measure of how confident each prediction is—to decide which classifier to trust, instead of retraining the model.
lead: When you learn a new skill after mastering a previous one, you risk forgetting what you already know. In machine learning, the same problem (called catastrophic forgetting) happens when a model learns new 3D object classes from just a handful of examples. Point-UQ solves this by measuring how confident each prediction is and using that confidence to choose the right decision-maker for each new object—without ever retraining the entire model.

problem.h2: The trap: hold old knowledge or grasp new classes
paras: You have a 3D object recognizer trained on 1000 photos of cars, chairs, and tables. A beginner's approach: download a few photos of a new object (say, lamps) and retrain the model to recognize lamps. Result: the model now recognizes lamps well but forgets what cars looked like. You have catastrophic forgetting.

The alternative: do not retrain. Just use the existing model to classify the lamp photos. Result: the model misses the lamp—it is still tuned for cars and chairs. So you are stuck between erasing old knowledge and ignoring new classes.

callout.html: The paper measures how uncertain each prediction is and uses that doubt to decide which classifier to consult—semantic rules or geometric shape—so old knowledge survives and new classes work.

steps.text: Take the 3D point cloud and extract details at coarse and fine scales, then blend them.
Ask the model to guess each point's class. How spread out are the scores across all classes? Spread out means uncertain.
If the scores are spread out, the model doubts itself. Route that sample to shape-based matching instead.
The learned classifier (trained on cars and chairs) never gets retrained. It stays frozen.
New lamp samples, routed to shape matching, form an average shape that sits alongside the old classifiers. No forgetting.

paras: The paper does not retrain or fine-tune the model. Instead, it swaps the decision rule: from trusting one fixed classifier to dynamically choosing between two classifiers based on how uncertain the model is about each sample.

hidden.h2: Entropy: how spread out is the guess
hidden.name: prediction entropy
paras: Entropy (a measure called prediction entropy) is a number that tells you how spread-out a prediction is. Imagine the model has a list of confidence scores for every possible class—car (0.8), chair (0.15), lamp (0.05). When one class dominates, entropy is low; the model is certain. When the scores are evenly distributed (car 0.33, chair 0.33, lamp 0.34), entropy is high; the model is confused.

The paper uses entropy to detect when the model is uncertain: when entropy is high, the model has seen few examples of this object and should not trust its learned classifier. It should instead ask about the object's 3D shape.

heat.caption: Darker cells are more uncertain or active. Spread measure (highlighted) triggers the route choice.

reads.html: Imagine guessing someone's height from a single photo. If that photo is blurry (high spread), you should not trust your guess; ask their friends instead (check their average height). If the photo is crystal clear, your guess alone is reliable (use what you learned).

Prediction spread (entropy) measures how evenly the model's confidence is distributed across classes. High spread means the model outputs nearly equal probabilities for all classes (confused). Low spread means one class dominates (confident). The paper measures this when answering each new question and uses it to pick the classifier.

paras: The mechanism is a division of labor. The learned classifier (trained on thousands of car and chair images) makes predictions by recognizing learned patterns—shapes, textures, edges. It works well on known objects but fails when given new objects it has never seen, because when spread is high, those predictions are unreliable.

A shape prototype is different: it stores the average 3D shape of each new class. When spread is high (meaning the sample is unfamiliar), the model stops trusting the learned classifier and asks instead: how close is this 3D point cloud to the average shape of a lamp? This avoids the retraining trap because the shape prototype does not change the learned patterns in the original classifier.

The two modules work together: one fuses coarse and fine details and outputs both the spread and a refined representation. The second one uses spread to pick the right classifier—if spread is low, use the learned patterns; if high, use shape matching. This keeps old classes untouched while new classes grow through shape prototypes.

stages.s: 3D point cloud (car, chair, or new lamp)
Fuse features at multiple scales into one representation
Compute spread: how confident is the prediction?
Is spread high? Route to shape matching. Otherwise route to learned classifier.
Prediction with no retraining, no forgetting

math.words: entropy = negative sum over all classes of (probability times log of probability). When entropy exceeds a threshold, route to geometric prototype instead of semantic classifier.
math.equation: spread(p) = -sum_c p_c * log(p_c); if spread(p) > threshold then use_shape = true else use_learned = true
symbols: the model's probability that the sample belongs to class c
the spread (entropy) of the probability distribution across all classes
a cutoff value; samples with spread above this are routed to shape matching
a yes/no flag: should we ask the shape prototype for the answer?
a yes/no flag: should we ask the learned classifier?

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Example 1: Predicting a car (model has seen many cars).
Threshold = 0.70. Since 0.52 is less than 0.70, use learned classifier (low spread, confident).
Example 2: Predicting a lamp (model has seen only three lamp photos).
Threshold = 0.70. Since 1.08 is greater than 0.70, use shape prototype (high spread, uncertain). The prototype matches the lamp's 3D shape without retraining the learned classifier.

math.note: Spread is the pull-cord: when the model doubts itself, it stops trusting learned patterns and leans instead on the average 3D shape.

charts.title: Naive fine-tuning
charts.note: The model learns lamps but forgets cars. Retraining the entire model erases old patterns.

charts.title: Point-UQ (this paper)
charts.note: By routing high-spread lamps to shape matching instead of retraining the learned classifier, car knowledge stays intact and lamps are still recognized well.

items.html: If the spread threshold is set too low, almost every sample routes to shape matching. The learned classifier is barely used. New classes work, but you lose the benefit of learned base-class patterns.
If the threshold is set too high, almost every sample trusts the learned classifier. New classes look like noise; the shape prototypes never get a chance to distinguish them.

The method works only if the few new examples are representative. A lamp prototype built from three photos of desk lamps might fail on floor lamps because those three samples do not cover the shape variety.
The paper sets the threshold adaptively using test samples from new classes and shows the method finds a sweet spot that lets both classifiers contribute.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a 3D point-cloud classifier trained on ModelNet (cars, chairs, tables). Freeze it. Download a few photos of a new object (say, a vase or a lamp). Without retraining, measure: (1) does the model still recognize the old objects (cars)? (2) does it now recognize the new object (vase)? Show that spread correctly identifies unfamiliar samples and routes them to shape matching.
demo.closing: The demo must make obvious that spread is the hinge: when you plot spread versus correct routing (did it pick the right classifier?), high spread samples should cluster on the shape-matching branch and low spread on the learned branch, with no retrained weights in between.
